    AI Overview
    base
    /bās/
    A base in chemistry is a substance that neutralizes acids, produces hydroxide ions (
    OH−OH raised to the negative power
    ) in aqueous solutions, and typically tastes bitter, feels slippery, and turns red litmus paper blue. Bases have a pH greater than 7, with strong bases having high pH values. They play a crucial role in chemical reactions, acting as proton acceptors. 
    Types of Bases 
    • Arrhenius Bases: Produce hydroxide ions (
      OH−OH raised to the negative power
      ) in water (e.g., Sodium Hydroxide -
      NaOHNaOH
      ).
    • Brønsted-Lowry Bases: Accept hydrogen ions (
      H+cap H raised to the positive power
      ).
    • Lewis Bases: Donate electron pairs.
    • Strong vs. Weak: Strong bases (like
      NaOHNaOH
       or
      KOHKOH
      ) dissociate completely, while weak bases (like ammonia,
      NH3NH sub 3
      ) do not.       
    Properties and Role 
    • pH Range: A base has a pH greater than 7, generally ranging from 7.1 to 14.
    • Properties: Slippery/soapy texture, bitter taste, and changes indicator colors (e.g., litmus to blue).
    • Role: Neutralizes acids to form water and salt, and is used in industrial, chemical, and biological applications.
    • Etymology: Derived from the concept that these compounds form the "base" (foundation) for creating salts when reacting with acids. 
    Common Examples 
    • Sodium Hydroxide (
      NaOHNaOH
      ):       Commonly known as lye.
    • Ammonia (
      NH3NH sub 3
      ):       A common weak base.
    • Calcium Hydroxide (
      Ca(OH)2Ca(OH) sub 2
      ):       Used in construction.
    • Magnesium Hydroxide (
      Mg(OH)2Mg(OH) sub 2
      ):       Used in antacids.

    Properties. What are the properties of a base in chemistry?
    About this result
    Feedback
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    Bases in chemistry are substances that feel slippery, taste bitter (though never taste in a lab!), turn red litmus paper blue, and have a pH above 7, often acting as electrolytes that conduct electricity in water by increasing hydroxide ion (
    OH−cap O cap H raised to the negative power
    )     concentration, neutralizing acids, and breaking down oils and fats.         Common examples include soaps, ammonia, and antacids, which utilize these properties for cleaning and buffering.
     
    Physical Properties
    • Feel: Slippery or soapy to the touch (e.g., soap). 
    • Taste: Bitter (avoid tasting in a lab!). 
    • pH: Above 7 (alkaline). 
    • Conductivity: Conduct electricity in aqueous solutions (electrolytes). 
    • Indicator Colors: Turn red litmus blue, phenolphthalein pink, and methyl orange yellow. 
    Chemical Properties
    • Hydroxide Production: Produce hydroxide ions (
      OH−cap O cap H raised to the negative power
      )       in water, increasing their concentration.       
    • Neutralization: React with acids to form salt and water. 
    • Reaction with Metals: React with some metals (like zinc) to produce hydrogen gas.
    • Reaction with Non-metals: React with non-metallic oxides (which are acidic) to form salt and water. 
    • Strength: Can be strong (dissociate completely, e.g., NaOH) or weak (partial dissociation, e.g., ammonia). 
    • Corrosiveness: Strong bases are corrosive to organic materials, fats, and oils, making them good cleaning agents. 
    Examples in Daily Life
    • Soaps & Detergents: Used for cleaning due to their ability to break down oils.
    • Antacids: Like Tums or Milk of Magnesia, used to neutralize stomach acid. 
    • Ammonia: Found in many household cleaners.

      PH Range. What is the pH range of a base?
      About this result
      Feedback
      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      A base has a pH range greater than 7 up to 14, with values closer to 14 indicating stronger basic (alkaline) properties, while anything below 7 is acidic, and exactly 7 is neutral.
       
      Key pH Scale Points: 
      • 0-6.9: Acidic (e.g., stomach acid, vinegar).
      • 7.0: Neutral (e.g., pure water).
      • 7.1-14: Basic/Alkaline (e.g., baking soda, ammonia, bleach).
      How it Works:
      • The pH scale measures the concentration of hydrogen ions (H+) and hydroxide ions (OH-) in a solution. 
      • Bases have more hydroxide ions than hydrogen ions, making them alkaline. 
      • Each whole number on the scale represents a tenfold change in acidity or basicity, meaning a pH of 10 is ten times more basic than a pH of 9, say the City of St Helens Oregon and the U.S. Geological Survey notes that pH is reported in logarithmic units.
